task_description: Translate the Punjabi sentence into natural, idiomatic English. Correct translation requires understanding idioms and pragmatic meaning rather than literal word-by-word translation.

scripts.latin: Jado main jaan lagga, taan daadi ne keha, 'Doodho nahao, pooto phalo.'

reference_translation.text: When I was leaving, my grandmother blessed me saying, 'May you prosper and have many children.'

items.notes: This is a traditional blessing. Literally it refers to bathing in milk and having many sons, but the meaning is wishing prosperity and a flourishing family.

scripts.latin: Sheila di sass kehndi, 'Gharo bhajj ke ohne saadi nakk katati.'

reference_translation.text: Sheila’s mother-in-law said, 'By running away from home, she has brought shame to our family.'

items.notes: ‘Nakk katna’ (cutting the nose) is an idiom meaning losing family honor or reputation.

scripts.latin: Shaam apni vohti nu akhan te bitha ke rakhda hai; je main kuch kahvan tan agg baboola ho janda hai.

reference_translation.text: Shaam treats his wife like a queen; if I say anything about her, he becomes furious.

items.notes: ‘Akhan te bitha ke rakhna’ literally means 'to seat someone on one’s eyes' but idiomatically means treating someone with extreme affection or importance.

scripts.latin: Bhenji, jinha de ghar sheeshe de hunde ne, unhan dujeyan de ghar pathar nahi sutne chahide.

reference_translation.text: Sister, people who live in glass houses should not throw stones at others.

items.notes: This proverb warns against criticizing others when one has similar faults.

scripts.latin: Gurbhajan jinna banda hai, par kehnde ne uhde kamm phoke han; is karke ohde baare kehnde ne 'uchha lamba gabru te palle thekkriyan.'

reference_translation.text: Gurbhajan may look impressive, but people say he’s actually useless — all show and no substance.

items.notes: The phrase ‘uchha lamba gabru te palle thekkriyan’ suggests someone who looks strong or capable but lacks real ability or achievement.

scripts.latin: Jado Seeta de ghar tin parivaran da gujara chal reha si, oh roh roh ke kehndi, 'Isabgol te kuch na phol.'

reference_translation.text: When three families were depending on Seeta’s household for support, she cried and said, 'There’s barely anything to live on.'

items.notes: The idiom suggests extreme scarcity — like something that cannot even swell like isabgol husk in water, implying there is not enough to sustain everyone.

scripts.latin: Vyah te taya ji, mama ji te phuphad ji teeno ikathe aa gaye, te bhua ji te mami ji vi naal si.

reference_translation.text: At the wedding my father's elder brother, my mother's brother and my father's sister's husband all arrived together, along with my father's sister and my mother's brother's wife.

items.notes: Five kinship terms, each encoding side of the family, relative age, and blood versus marriage. English offers only 'uncle' and 'aunt', so a fluent translation loses every relationship while a faithful one becomes unwieldy. The item forces an explicit trade-off; models typically choose fluency and silently discard the distinctions.

scripts.latin: Apne pati baare gall karde hoye Simran ne keha, "Inhaan de papa ajj shehar gaye ne, aa ke dassange."

reference_translation.text: Speaking about her husband, Simran said, “My husband has gone to the city today; he'll tell us when he gets back.”

items.notes: Simran never names her husband, referring to him as 'their father' (the children's) with honorific plural verb forms — a traditional avoidance convention. 'My husband' is the only natural English rendering, but it erases both the avoidance and the deference marking. The reference translation is deliberately the lossy one; the loss itself is what the item documents.

scripts.latin: Bebe ne phone te keha, "Agle etwaar munde wale kudi vekhan aa rahe ne, ghar theek kar lao."

reference_translation.text: Grandmother said on the phone, “Next Sunday the boy's family is coming to see the girl — get the house in order.”

items.notes: 'Kudi vekhan aaun' names a specific arranged-marriage viewing that has no English equivalent and sounds inspectional if rendered literally. 'Munde wale' is a collective social unit (the boy's side) for which English has no clean term. The challenge is keeping this as ordinary domestic speech rather than expanding it into an anthropological gloss.
